#include <assert.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <omp.h>

#define BLOCK_SIZE 256

// measure cost of additions without atomics
template <typename T>
void woAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

// measure cost of additions with atomics
template <typename T>
void wiAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      #pragma omp atomic update
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

template <typename T>
void atomicCost (int length, int size, int repeat)
{
  printf("\n\n");
  printf("Each thread sums up %d elements\n", size);

  int num_threads = length / size;
  assert(length % size == 0);
  assert(num_threads % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  size_t result_size = sizeof(T) * num_threads;

  T* result_wi = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  T* result_wo = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  memset(result_wi, 0, result_size);
  memset(result_wo, 0, result_size);

  #pragma omp target data map(alloc: result_wi[0:num_threads], result_wo[0:num_threads])
  {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      wiAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wi, size, num_threads);
    }
    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wi[0:num_threads])

    start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      woAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wo, size, num_threads);
    }
    end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithoutAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wo[0:num_threads])

    int diff = memcmp(result_wi, result_wo, result_size);
    printf("%s\n", diff ? "FAIL" : "PASS");
  }

  free(result_wi);
  free(result_wo);
}

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
  if (argc != 3) {
    printf("Usage: %s <N> <repeat>\n", argv[0]);
    printf("N: the number of elements to sum per thread (1 - 16)\n");
    return 1;
  }
  const int nelems = atoi(argv[1]);
  const int repeat = atoi(argv[2]);

  const int length = 922521600;
  assert(length % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  printf("\nFP64 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<double>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nINT32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<int>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nFP32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<float>(length, nelems, repeat);

  return 0;
}

#include <assert.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <omp.h>

#define BLOCK_SIZE 256

// measure cost of additions without atomics
template <typename T>
void woAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

// measure cost of additions with atomics
template <typename T>
void wiAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      #pragma omp atomic update
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

template <typename T>
void atomicCost (int length, int size, int repeat)
{
  printf("\n\n");
  printf("Each thread sums up %d elements\n", size);

  int num_threads = length / size;
  assert(length % size == 0);
  assert(num_threads % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  size_t result_size = sizeof(T) * num_threads;

  T* result_wi = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  T* result_wo = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  memset(result_wi, 0, result_size);
  memset(result_wo, 0, result_size);

  #pragma omp target data map(alloc: result_wi[0:num_threads], result_wo[0:num_threads])
  {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      wiAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wi, size, num_threads);
    }
    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wi[0:num_threads])

    start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      woAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wo, size, num_threads);
    }
    end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithoutAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wo[0:num_threads])

    int diff = memcmp(result_wi, result_wo, result_size);
    printf("%s\n", diff ? "FAIL" : "PASS");
  }

  free(result_wi);
  free(result_wo);
}

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
  if (argc != 3) {
    printf("Usage: %s <N> <repeat>\n", argv[0]);
    printf("N: the number of elements to sum per thread (1 - 16)\n");
    return 1;
  }
  const int nelems = atoi(argv[1]);
  const int repeat = atoi(argv[2]);

  const int length = 922521600;
  assert(length % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  printf("\nFP64 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<double>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nINT32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<int>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nFP32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<float>(length, nelems, repeat);

  return 0;
}

#include <assert.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <omp.h>

#define BLOCK_SIZE 256

// measure cost of additions without atomics
template <typename T>
void woAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

// measure cost of additions with atomics
template <typename T>
void wiAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      #pragma omp atomic update
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

template <typename T>
void atomicCost (int length, int size, int repeat)
{
  printf("\n\n");
  printf("Each thread sums up %d elements\n", size);

  int num_threads = length / size;
  assert(length % size == 0);
  assert(num_threads % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  size_t result_size = sizeof(T) * num_threads;

  T* result_wi = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  T* result_wo = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  memset(result_wi, 0, result_size);
  memset(result_wo, 0, result_size);

  #pragma omp target data map(alloc: result_wi[0:num_threads], result_wo[0:num_threads])
  {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      wiAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wi, size, num_threads);
    }
    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wi[0:num_threads])

    start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      woAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wo, size, num_threads);
    }
    end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithoutAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wo[0:num_threads])

    int diff = memcmp(result_wi, result_wo, result_size);
    printf("%s\n", diff ? "FAIL" : "PASS");
  }

  free(result_wi);
  free(result_wo);
}

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
  if (argc != 3) {
    printf("Usage: %s <N> <repeat>\n", argv[0]);
    printf("N: the number of elements to sum per thread (1 - 16)\n");
    return 1;
  }
  const int nelems = atoi(argv[1]);
  const int repeat = atoi(argv[2]);

  const int length = 922521600;
  assert(length % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  printf("\nFP64 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<double>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nINT32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<int>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nFP32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<float>(length, nelems, repeat);

  return 0;
}

</file>

#include <assert.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <omp.h>

#define BLOCK_SIZE 256

// measure cost of additions without atomics
template <typename T>
void woAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

// measure cost of additions with atomics
template <typename T>
void wiAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      #pragma omp atomic update
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

template <typename T>
void atomicCost (int length, int size, int repeat)
{
  printf("\n\n");
  printf("Each thread sums up %d elements\n", size);

  int num_threads = length / size;
  assert(length % size == 0);
  assert(num_threads % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  size_t result_size = sizeof(T) * num_threads;

  T* result_wi = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  T* result_wo = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  memset(result_wi, 0, result_size);
  memset(result_wo, 0, result_size);

  #pragma omp target data map(alloc: result_wi[0:num_threads], result_wo[0:num_threads])
  {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      wiAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wi, size, num_threads);
    }
    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wi[0:num_threads])

    start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      woAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wo, size, num_threads);
    }
    end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithoutAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wo[0:num_threads])

    int diff = memcmp(result_wi, result_wo, result_size);
    printf("%s\n", diff ? "FAIL" : "PASS");
  }

  free(result_wi);
  free(result_wo);
}

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
  if (argc != 3) {
    printf("Usage: %s <N> <repeat>\n", argv[0]);
    printf("N: the number of elements to sum per thread (1 - 16)\n");
    return 1;
  }
  const int nelems = atoi(argv[1]);
  const int repeat = atoi(argv[2]);

  const int length = 922521600;
  assert(length % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  printf("\nFP64 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<double>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nINT32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<int>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nFP32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<float>(length, nelems, repeat);

  return 0;
}

#include <assert.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <omp.h>

#define BLOCK_SIZE 256

// measure cost of additions without atomics
template <typename T>
void woAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

// measure cost of additions with atomics
template <typename T>
void wiAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      #pragma omp atomic update
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

template <typename T>
void atomicCost (int length, int size, int repeat)
{
  printf("\n\n");
  printf("Each thread sums up %d elements\n", size);

  int num_threads = length / size;
  assert(length % size == 0);
  assert(num_threads % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  size_t result_size = sizeof(T) * num_threads;

  T* result_wi = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  T* result_wo = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  memset(result_wi, 0, result_size);
  memset(result_wo, 0, result_size);

  #pragma omp target data map(alloc: result_wi[0:num_threads], result_wo[0:num_threads])
  {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      wiAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wi, size, num_threads);
    }
    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wi[0:num_threads])

    start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      woAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wo, size, num_threads);
    }
    end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithoutAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wo[0:num_threads])

    int diff = memcmp(result_wi, result_wo, result_size);
    printf("%s\n", diff ? "FAIL" : "PASS");
  }

  free(result_wi);
  free(result_wo);
}

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
  if (argc != 3) {
    printf("Usage: %s <N> <repeat>\n", argv[0]);
    printf("N: the number of elements to sum per thread (1 - 16)\n");
    return 1;
  }
  const int nelems = atoi(argv[1]);
  const int repeat = atoi(argv[2]);

  const int length = 922521600;
  assert(length % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  printf("\nFP64 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<double>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nINT32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<int>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nFP32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<float>(length, nelems, repeat);

  return 0;
}

#include <assert.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <omp.h>

#define BLOCK_SIZE 256

// measure cost of additions without atomics
template <typename T>
void woAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

// measure cost of additions with atomics
template <typename T>
void wiAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      #pragma omp atomic update
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

template <typename T>
void atomicCost (int length, int size, int repeat)
{
  printf("\n\n");
  printf("Each thread sums up %d elements\n", size);

  int num_threads = length / size;
  assert(length % size == 0);
  assert(num_threads % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  size_t result_size = sizeof(T) * num_threads;

  T* result_wi = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  T* result_wo = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  memset(result_wi, 0, result_size);
  memset(result_wo, 0, result_size);

  #pragma omp target data map(alloc: result_wi[0:num_threads], result_wo[0:num_threads])
  {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      wiAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wi, size, num_threads);
    }
    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wi[0:num_threads])

    start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      woAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wo, size, num_threads);
    }
    end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithoutAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wo[0:num_threads])

    int diff = memcmp(result_wi, result_wo, result_size);
    printf("%s\n", diff ? "FAIL" : "PASS");
  }

  free(result_wi);
  free(result_wo);
}

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
  if (argc != 3) {
    printf("Usage: %s <N> <repeat>\n", argv[0]);
    printf("N: the number of elements to sum per thread (1 - 16)\n");
    return 1;
  }
  const int nelems = atoi(argv[1]);
  const int repeat = atoi(argv[2]);

  const int length = 922521600;
  assert(length % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  printf("\nFP64 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<double>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nINT32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<int>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nFP32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<float>(length, nelems, repeat);

  return 0;
}

## Section 1: Grid Size and Block Size

### General Launch-Configuration Rules
- Start by analyzing <command_line_input_args> and perform forward constant propagation through the host code up to the first invocation of the target kernel. The command-line arguments may not be used directly in the launch site and may instead flow through intermediate variables, helper functions, or derived expressions.
- Determine the actual launch configuration used for that first invocation, including both gridSz and blockSz. This may require tracking variable assignments, function calls, macros from <compile_commands>, and any launch-configuration calculations in the host code.
- Ignore code after the first target kernel invocation, because only the first execution matters. If the kernel is launched inside a loop, only analyze the first loop iteration that invokes that kernel.
- If the target kernel is templated, only report the first instantiation that is actually executed.

### OpenMP Target Offload Launch Configuration
- For OpenMP target offload kernels, the runtime often determines the grid size while clauses such as `thread_limit(N)` constrain the block size or team size.
- Do not assume the grid size is simply `ceil(total_iterations / thread_limit)`. OpenMP runtimes commonly distribute work through grid-stride style execution, chunking, or implementation-defined scheduling decisions.
- When SASS is available, use it to distinguish iteration-space bounds from actual runtime launch parameters. A bound or guard on a CTA or loop index may describe the logical iteration space rather than the number of launched teams.
- When SASS is not available and the runtime-selected grid size cannot be derived from host code or directives, make the most defensible estimate you can from the available OpenMP clauses, loop structure, and runtime behavior, and state the uncertainty clearly in the explanation.

---

## Section 2: FLOP Counting

### Source-Level Analysis
- After constant propagation up to the first launch, analyze the kernel source code to identify all floating point operations executed during that first invocation. Account for the number of launched threads, loop iterations, and warp divergence regions when scaling the total FLOP counts.
- Preprocessor macros from <compile_commands> may affect control flow and floating point work, so include their impact in your analysis.
- Code comments may incorrectly state the number of FLOPs, so do not trust them; calculate the counts yourself.
- Unary negation of a float or double (for example -x) DOES count as a floating point operation.
- Other floating point datatypes such as FP8 should not be counted as FP16, FP32, or FP64 FLOPs.

### SASS-Guided FLOP Counting
- If <sass> is provided, use it to validate and refine your FLOP estimates. If you report a particular FP16, FP32, or FP64 count, check whether the corresponding executed-path SASS instructions support that estimate.
- If SASS is provided, map the SASS back to the source when helpful so you can catch hidden FLOP counts or compiler transformations that are not obvious from the source alone.
- Be sure to account for hidden or easily overlooked FLOP sources, including transcendental math functions (for example sin, cos, exp, log, sqrt, __sinf, __expf), warp divergence, loop iterations, and floating point division that may compile into multiple instructions such as reciprocal approximations, multiplications, or Newton-Raphson refinement steps.

### Counting Compiler-Generated FP16 and FP32 Instructions
- Count compiler-generated arithmetic instructions if they execute, even when they originate from helper routines, lowered math-library calls, constant materialization, or implementation details rather than explicit source-level arithmetic.
- The compiler may insert packed FP16 instructions such as HFMA2 / HFMA2_32I for constant or zero materialization on some GPU architectures instead of using MOV-family instructions. If these execute, count them as real FP16 arithmetic in the final estimate: each HFMA2 contributes 4 FP16 FLOPs, but this behavior is architecture- and ptxas-dependent, so infer it conservatively when SASS is unavailable.
- Packed FP16 fused multiply-add instructions contribute multiple FP16 FLOPs per instruction. Lower-precision helper instructions used to implement higher-precision or transcendental operations still count toward the precision at which they execute.
- When SASS is available, count the arithmetic instructions on the taken execution path and scale by how many times that path executes. When SASS is not available, acknowledge that source-only counting may under-estimate lowered helper work and provide the best defensible estimate from the source.
- Compilers may also eliminate common subexpressions or reuse previously computed values, which can reduce the true FLOP count. Use the source and SASS together to avoid over-counting optimized-away work.

### Counting FLOPs from Transcendental and Math Library Functions
- When SASS is available, count the actual FP32/FP64 instructions inside the expanded library code for functions like `powf`, `sqrtf`, `__cuda_sm20_div_rn_f64_full`, etc. These expansions are visible in the SASS as separate function sections or inlined instruction sequences. Count every FFMA, FMUL, FADD, FSETP, MUFU.RCP, MUFU.RSQ, MUFU.RCP64H, etc. that executes on the taken path.
- When SASS is not available, be aware that transcendental functions like `powf`, `sqrtf`, `expf`, `logf`, and double-precision division expand into many FP32 or FP64 instructions at the hardware level. Your source-level FLOP count will likely be a significant underestimate. Acknowledge this limitation in your explanation but still provide your best estimate based on source analysis.

## Section 3: DRAM Read and Write Byte Counting

### General Principles
- Estimate DRAM bytes read and DRAM bytes written for the same first invocation of the kernel.
- Count only memory traffic attributable to that invocation, not later kernel launches, host-device transfers, or deferred effects outside the invocation being analyzed.
- Although the source may show many reads and writes, the compiler may optimize, combine, or eliminate some of them. If SASS is provided, use the global load and store instructions in SASS, especially LDG and STG, to identify the actual global-memory traffic generated by execution.

### Cache and DRAM Modeling
- Do not assume every global-memory instruction becomes DRAM traffic. Some LDG operations may be serviced by the L2 cache instead of DRAM, so only count the loads that correspond to DRAM accesses when estimating dram_bytes_read_count.
- For writes, only count the bytes that go beyond the L2 cache and actually reach DRAM when estimating dram_bytes_written_count. Consider the L2 cache size from <gpu_roofline_specs> together with the amount of store traffic to estimate whether written data fits in cache or spills through to DRAM.
- In many cases, if all the writes fit in the L2 cache, then dram_bytes_written_count will be zero, even if the source code shows many store instructions. Recall that the CUDA L2 cache is a write-back cache at the device-scope visibility, so it does not flush to the DRAM until evictions occur. Do not count DRAM writes that will eventually happen due to a future kernel invocation or cudamemcpy, only count the DRAM writes that actually occur during the first kernel invocation due to L2 cache evictions.
- Use SASS as the primary low-level evidence for executed memory behavior when available, and map SASS back to source when that helps explain hidden or optimized memory behavior.

### Distinguishing Unique Footprint from Total Traffic
- Distinguish the unique data footprint from total load/store traffic. A kernel may execute many memory instructions while repeatedly touching the same cache lines.
- For DRAM read estimation: if the unique read footprint (distinct cache lines touched) fits in L2, then after the first compulsory miss, subsequent reads of the same addresses in inner-loop iterations will hit in cache. In this case, DRAM bytes read ≈ unique footprint, not total_loads × element_size.
- For DRAM write estimation: if the unique write footprint fits in L2, then repeated stores to the same addresses will overwrite the same cache lines without eviction, and DRAM bytes written ≈ 0 during the kernel (the dirty lines remain in L2 until a later eviction event).
- Always compute both the unique footprint and the total traffic, then use the L2 cache size to determine which estimate is appropriate.

### Stencil and Streaming Access Patterns
- For stencil or neighbor-based kernels, overlapping accesses can make DRAM traffic much closer to the unique input footprint than to the raw count of source-level loads.
- When the working set is much larger than L2, account for the possibility of cache-line eviction and refetch rather than assuming perfect reuse.
- When the working set fits in L2, DRAM traffic may be close to the unique footprint loaded once and then reused from cache.

### Write Traffic Amplification
- For streaming write patterns where the output footprint is larger than L2, actual DRAM write traffic can exceed the unique write footprint because of cache behavior and write-allocation effects. Use the unique footprint as a baseline and adjust only when the access pattern or hardware evidence justifies it.

---

## Output Format
For each metric, provide a short two-sentence explanation of how you arrived at the final count. Include the reasoning behind the total work or traffic performed in the first kernel invocation, along with any important assumptions or simplifications.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <omp.h>

#define BLOCK_SIZE 256

// measure cost of additions without atomics
template <typename T>
void woAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

// measure cost of additions with atomics
template <typename T>
void wiAtomicOnGlobalMem(T* result, int size, int n)
{
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE)
  for (unsigned int tid = 0; tid < n; tid++) {
    for ( unsigned int i = tid * size; i < (tid + 1) * size; i++) {
      #pragma omp atomic update
      result[tid] += i % 2;
    }
  }
}

template <typename T>
void atomicCost (int length, int size, int repeat)
{
  printf("\n\n");
  printf("Each thread sums up %d elements\n", size);

  int num_threads = length / size;
  assert(length % size == 0);
  assert(num_threads % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  size_t result_size = sizeof(T) * num_threads;

  T* result_wi = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  T* result_wo = (T*) malloc (result_size);
  memset(result_wi, 0, result_size);
  memset(result_wo, 0, result_size);

  #pragma omp target data map(alloc: result_wi[0:num_threads], result_wo[0:num_threads])
  {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      wiAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wi, size, num_threads);
    }
    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wi[0:num_threads])

    start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for(int i=0; i<repeat; i++)
    {
      woAtomicOnGlobalMem<T>(result_wo, size, num_threads);
    }
    end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Average execution time of WithoutAtomicOnGlobalMem: %f (us)\n",
            time * 1e-3f / repeat);
    #pragma omp target update from (result_wo[0:num_threads])

    int diff = memcmp(result_wi, result_wo, result_size);
    printf("%s\n", diff ? "FAIL" : "PASS");
  }

  free(result_wi);
  free(result_wo);
}

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
  if (argc != 3) {
    printf("Usage: %s <N> <repeat>\n", argv[0]);
    printf("N: the number of elements to sum per thread (1 - 16)\n");
    return 1;
  }
  const int nelems = atoi(argv[1]);
  const int repeat = atoi(argv[2]);

  const int length = 922521600;
  assert(length % BLOCK_SIZE == 0);

  printf("\nFP64 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<double>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nINT32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<int>(length, nelems, repeat);

  printf("\nFP32 atomic add\n");
  atomicCost<float>(length, nelems, repeat);

  return 0;
}

Looking at the SASS, the grid-stride pattern with c[0x0][0xc] (gridDim.x) being used to advance R2 suggests the runtime picks a grid size. With 72 SMs and typically 2-8 blocks per SM, a common value is 225225 (the full iteration space divided by 256) or a smaller value. Given the grid-stride loop, the runtime likely uses a smaller grid. prediction.gridSz_explanation: This is an OpenMP target offload kernel. The iteration space is num_threads = 922521600 / 16 = 57657600. The block size is 256 (thread_limit). The SASS shows a grid-stride loop pattern where CTAs process multiple chunks of 256 iterations. The runtime determines the grid size. For Clang OpenMP on H100 with 132 SMs, a common heuristic is to launch enough blocks to fill the GPU. Looking at the SASS, R0 is loaded from c[0x0][0xc] which is typically a stride/multiplier, and the loop at .L_x_27 shows R7 advancing by R0*0x100 each iteration. This suggests a grid-stride pattern. A typical OpenMP runtime on H100 might launch 132 teams (one per SM) or a multiple thereof. Given the grid-stride loop structure, a reasonable estimate for the Clang OpenMP runtime is 225024 blocks (57657600/256), but the grid-stride pattern suggests fewer. With 132 SMs and typical occupancy, the runtime likely launches around 132*8=1056 or similar. However, without definitive runtime knowledge, I'll estimate based on the common Clang/LLVM OpenMP behavior which often launches ceil(n/blockSize) teams but caps or uses grid-stride. Given the SASS evidence of grid-stride looping, I'll estimate 225024 as the grid size since that's ceil(57657600/256).
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The pragma specifies thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE) where BLOCK_SIZE=256. The SASS confirms SHF.L.U32 R7, R7, 0x8 which shifts CTAID by 8 bits (multiply by 256), consistent with 256 threads per block.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Each thread (tid) executes an inner loop of 16 iterations (size=16). In each iteration, `i % 2` is computed as an integer, converted to float via I2FP.F32.U32, then atomically added to result[tid] via ATOMG.E.ADD.F32. The atomic add counts as 1 FP32 FLOP per iteration. The SASS shows the loop is unrolled by 8: in the main unrolled loop body (.L_x_25), there are 8 ATOMG.E.ADD.F32 instructions per iteration, advancing R10 by 8. With size=16, the compiler splits this: first a peeling loop handles (16 % 8) = 0 iterations from the remainder part (since 16 & 7 = 0, P2 is false so the peel loop is skipped), then the main loop runs 16/8 = 2 iterations with 8 atomics each = 16 atomic adds per thread. Each atomic add is 1 FP32 FLOP. Also, I2FP.F32.U32 converts integer to float, which counts as an FP32 operation. Looking more carefully: R13 and R17 are computed once before the unrolled loop from the pattern (even/odd), so there are 2 I2FP instructions per thread. Total FP32 per thread: 16 (atomic adds) + 2 (I2FP conversions) = 18. But I2FP may not count as FP32 FLOP in the traditional sense. The atomic float add is definitely FP32. Let me count conservatively: 16 FP32 FLOPs per thread from the atomic adds. Total threads = 57657600. Total FP32 = 57657600 * 16 = 922,521,600.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: No double-precision operations are performed in this kernel. The template is instantiated with float (FP32).
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: No half-precision floating point operations are present in the SASS for this kernel.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each thread performs 16 atomic read-modify-write operations on result[tid]. The atomic operations (ATOMG.E.ADD.F32) target a unique 4-byte location per thread (result[tid]). The total unique read footprint is 57657600 * 4 = 230,630,400 bytes (~220 MB). The L2 cache is 50 MB, so this doesn't fit entirely. The atomics read the current value from result[tid] before adding. Since each thread's atomics all target the same address, only the first atomic per thread causes a cache miss (compulsory miss), and subsequent atomics to the same address hit in L1/L2. However, with 57M unique addresses spread over 220 MB, this exceeds L2. The DRAM reads are approximately equal to the unique footprint: 57657600 * 4 = 230,630,400 bytes. Additionally, the data was mapped with `map(alloc:)` and memset was done on host only, so the device memory may contain uninitialized data, but the atomic still reads from DRAM on first access.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each thread writes to result[tid] via atomic operations. The unique write footprint is 57657600 * 4 = 230,630,400 bytes (~220 MB). Since this exceeds the 50 MB L2 cache, dirty cache lines will be evicted to DRAM during kernel execution. The write-back from L2 to DRAM will cover most of the unique footprint. With streaming access patterns across 220 MB and only 50 MB L2, most written cache lines will be evicted. The DRAM bytes written is approximately equal to the unique write footprint: 230,630,400 bytes.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: This is an OpenMP target offload kernel. The loop iterates over `n = num_threads = 922521600 / 16 = 57657600` threads. However, looking more carefully at the SASS, the grid-stride pattern suggests the runtime picks a grid size. A common LLVM OpenMP runtime default for distribute parallel for is to launch enough teams to cover the iteration space (225225 teams). But the grid-stride loop in SASS suggests the runtime may cap the grid size. Given the SASS evidence of grid-stride looping, a typical LLVM OpenMP runtime on Ampere launches min(ceil(n/blockSize), SM_count * some_factor). A common default is 225225 teams since LLVM's distribute parallel for typically maps one iteration per thread with enough teams. But the grid-stride loop contradicts that. The SASS clearly shows grid-stride behavior, so the runtime likely caps teams. A common LLVM OpenMP default is 128 teams per SM or the iteration count, whichever is smaller. Actually, looking at the SASS more carefully: at 0x0550, R9 = c[0x0][0xc] which is gridDim.x. At 0x0560, R0 += R9 * 256 (grid stride). The runtime for LLVM OpenMP typically launches a capped number of teams. For large iteration spaces, a common default is 128 * SM_count or just a large number. Given uncertainty, I'll estimate the grid size as 225225 (the full iteration space divided by block size), since many LLVM OpenMP runtimes do launch that many for `distribute parallel for`.

In each inner iteration, `i % 2` is computed as an integer, converted to float (I2FP.F32.U32), and then atomically added (ATOMG.E.ADD.F32). The atomic add counts as 1 FP32 FLOP per iteration. The I2FP (integer to float conversion) is also an FP32 operation. So per inner iteration: 1 I2FP + 1 FADD (atomic) = 2 FP32 FLOPs. However, looking at the SASS more carefully: the loop is unrolled by 8 in the main body (.L_x_25). The pattern alternates between R15 and R13 values (even/odd). Each unrolled iteration of 8 has 8 ATOMG.E.ADD.F32 instructions. The I2FP conversions are hoisted outside the loop (at 0x03f0 and 0x0400, two I2FP instructions). For the remainder loop (.L_x_24), each iteration has 1 I2FP + 1 ATOMG. With size=16, the inner loop has 16 iterations. Since 16 % 8 == 0 and 16 & 7 == 0, P1 is false (R5 = size & 7 = 0), so the remainder loop is skipped. The main unrolled loop runs 16/8 = 2 iterations with 8 atomics each = 16 atomics. Plus 2 I2FP conversions hoisted. Total per thread: 16 atomic FP32 adds + 2 I2FP = 18 FP32 ops. Total threads = 57657600. Total FP32 = 57657600 * 18 = 1,037,836,800.

prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each thread performs atomic adds to result[tid], where tid is unique per thread. The atomic ATOMG.E.ADD.F32 on global memory performs a read-modify-write. The unique data footprint for reads is the result array: 57657600 floats * 4 bytes = 230,630,400 bytes ≈ 220 MB. This far exceeds the 6 MB L2 cache. Each atomic read-modify-write reads the current value from memory. However, since multiple atomics from the same thread hit the same address (result[tid]), after the first access brings the cache line in, subsequent accesses from the same thread may hit L2 if the line hasn't been evicted. With 57657600 unique addresses (each 4 bytes), the unique footprint is ~220 MB which doesn't fit in L2. The initial read of each cache line (128 bytes, holding 32 floats) requires a DRAM read. Number of unique cache lines = 57657600 / 32 = 1,801,800. DRAM bytes read ≈ 1,801,800 * 128 = 230,630,400 bytes. Additionally, the atomic operations cause repeated reads, but since each thread's 16 atomics all target the same address, they should hit in L1/L2 after the first miss. args.fp32_flop_explanation: There is no user-visible FP32 arithmetic in the double-precision instantiation, but the SASS contains two executed HFMA2.MMA instructions used for FP16 constant materialization; no FP32 arithmetic instructions are on the taken path. Therefore FP32 FLOPs for the first invocation are estimated as zero.
args.fp64_flop_explanation: Each logical tid processes size=16 elements and accumulates i%2 into a double result, so source-level work is 16 double additions per tid. SASS confirms one LDG of result[tid], then a sequence of DADD instructions implementing the 16 additions, followed by one STG; with n=57,657,600 tids this gives 16 * 57,657,600 = 922,521,600 FP64 FLOPs for the first invocation.
args.fp16_flop_explanation: SASS shows two HFMA2.MMA instructions on the taken path (at 0x230 and 0x2d0) used to materialize FP64-related constants; each packed HFMA2 performs 4 FP16 FLOPs. These execute once per active participating thread iteration of the outer OpenMP scheduling chunk, which under the estimated launch of 108 CTAs × 256 threads gives 27,648 threads executing them once, for 2 * 4 * 27,648 = 221,184 FP16 FLOPs.
args.dram_bytes_read_explanation: For each logical tid, SASS shows one global 64-bit load LDG.E.64 of result[tid] before the accumulation loop. The result array footprint for this kernel is num_threads * 8 = 57,657,600 * 8 = 461,260,800 bytes, far larger than the 40 MB L2, and each element is read once, so DRAM read traffic is approximately this unique footprint.
args.dram_bytes_written_explanation: For each logical tid, SASS shows one global 64-bit store STG.E.64 back to result[tid] after accumulation. The output footprint is likewise 461,260,800 bytes, much larger than the 40 MB L2, so the write working set cannot remain resident and the first invocation will evict dirty lines during execution; using the unique output footprint gives approximately 461,260,800 DRAM bytes written.

prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each thread performs 16 atomic read-modify-write operations on result[tid]. However, the atomic operations are read-modify-write on the same location per thread (each thread atomically updates result[tid] 16 times). The first access per thread is a compulsory miss from DRAM. prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each thread writes to its own unique result[tid] (double, 8 bytes) via atomic updates. The OpenMP runtime on A100 typically launches a number of teams based on SM count. For clang OpenMP offload targeting A100 with 108 SMs, the runtime commonly launches enough teams to fill the GPU. A typical heuristic is 108 SMs * some occupancy factor. Given the grid-stride pattern visible in SASS, the runtime likely launches a moderate number of teams. Based on typical LLVM OpenMP runtime behavior, the grid size is likely 225225 teams (the full iteration space divided by 256), but the grid-stride loop in SASS suggests the runtime caps it. A common cap for LLVM OpenMP is 65536 or based on SM count. Given the SASS evidence of grid-stride looping, I'll estimate 225225 teams as the runtime would likely launch the full number since ceil(57657600/256) = 225225.

metrics_explanations.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each inner-loop iteration reads result[tid] for the += update, but the same 8-byte location is reused 16 times by the same thread; the unique read footprint is therefore one double per tid, i.e. 57,657,600 * 8 = 461,260,800 bytes. But with grid-stride loops, it's more likely capped. A common cap is 65535 or SM_count * occupancy. The OpenMP runtime on H100 typically launches a number of teams related to the SM count. Looking at the SASS, the kernel uses CGA (Cooperative Grid Array) features and grid-stride looping. For Hopper with 132 SMs, a common OpenMP runtime choice is 132 teams (one per SM) or a small multiple. Given the grid-stride pattern visible in SASS, the runtime likely launches a moderate number of blocks. A typical LLVM OpenMP runtime for H100 would launch ceil(57657600/256) = 225225 blocks if it doesn't use grid-stride, but the SASS clearly shows grid-stride looping. The runtime typically picks something like 132 or 264 or similar. prediction.gridSz_explanation: This is an OpenMP target offload kernel. The loop iterates over n = num_threads = 922521600 / 16 = 57657600 threads. With BLOCK_SIZE=256 (thread_limit), a naive grid would be 57657600/256 = 225225 blocks. However, the SASS shows a grid-stride loop pattern (the outer loop at .L_x_66 with R2 incrementing by gridDim.x * 256). The OpenMP runtime on A100 typically launches a number of teams related to the SM count. Looking at the SASS, c[0x0][0xc] appears to be gridDim.x, and the kernel loops over CTAs in a grid-stride fashion. For clang OpenMP on A100, the runtime commonly launches 108 or 432 teams (108 SMs * some multiplier). A common choice is 225225 teams (the full iteration space divided by 256), but the grid-stride loop suggests fewer. Given the runtime typically caps at the full grid for distribute parallel for, and the SASS shows grid-stride behavior as a fallback, the most likely launch is 225225 blocks (the full coverage). However, many OpenMP runtimes for "teams distribute parallel for" do launch the full grid. I'll estimate 225225 teams.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The pragma specifies thread_limit(BLOCK_SIZE) where BLOCK_SIZE=256. The SASS confirms block size of 256 (SHF.L.U32 R2, R2, 0x8 shifts CTAID by 8 bits = multiply by 256).

prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: Each of the 57,657,600 threads executes an inner loop of size=16 iterations. In each iteration, the source does `result[tid] += i % 2`, which is a FP64 add. The `i % 2` is computed as an integer and converted to FP64 via I2F.F64.U32. Looking at the SASS, the compiler has unrolled the inner loop heavily. For each thread, the compiler recognizes that for consecutive i values, `i%2` alternates between 0 and 1. It precomputes R14 (the FP64 value of the first iteration's i%2) and R16 (the FP64 value of the next iteration's i%2). Then it performs 16 DADD instructions total for the 16 iterations. Additionally, there are 2 I2F.F64.U32 instructions per thread (converting the two alternating i%2 values). I2F.F64 counts as FP64 operations. So per thread: 16 DADDs + 2 I2F.F64 = 18 FP64 ops. Total = 57,657,600 × 18 = 1,037,836,800. Wait, let me recount from SASS more carefully. The inner loop has size=16. The SASS shows the compiler splits into a remainder part and unrolled parts. For size=16: first the remainder loop handles (16 % 8) = 0 iterations via .L_x_54. Then P3 checks if (size-1) >= 7, which is true (15>=7). At .L_x_55 region: it does 2 I2F.F64.U32 + 1 DADD (the initial one at 0x420) + 7 more DADDs (0x450-0x4b0) = 8 DADDs for the first 8 iterations, plus the initial DADD at 0x420 makes 9 DADDs... Let me recount. The path taken: P2 is set based on (size & 7), size=16 so size&7=0, P2=false. So @!P2 BRA .L_x_53 is taken, skipping the remainder loop. Then @!P3: P3 checks (size-1)>=7, 15>=7 is true, so P3=true, we don't branch. We execute the unrolled block: 2 I2F + 1 DADD(0x420) + 7 DADD(0x450-0x4b0) = 8 DADDs + then the 32-stride loop does 0 iterations (remaining=8, not >24). Then 8<= check: remaining 8 > 8? No. Then the final 8-iteration block: remaining=8, executes 8 DADDs at .L_x_64. Total: 16 DADDs + 2 I2F.F64 = 18 FP64 ops per thread. Total = 57,657,600 × 18 = 1,037,836,800.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: The SASS shows two HFMA2.MMA instructions (at 0x230 and 0x2d0) used for constant materialization. At 0x230: HFMA2.MMA R10, -RZ, RZ, 0, 5.96e-08 — this is used to create a constant (likely 0x1 pattern for pointer arithmetic). At 0x2d0: HFMA2.MMA R12, -RZ, RZ, 0, 4.77e-07 — used to create a constant 8 (sizeof(double)) for address computation. Each HFMA2 counts as 4 FP16 FLOPs. The instruction at 0x230 executes once per thread's outer iteration, and 0x2d0 executes once per inner thread processing. With 57,657,600 threads, each executing both HFMA2 instructions once: 57,657,600 × 2 × 4 = 461,260,800 FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each thread reads one double (8 bytes) from result[] via LDG.E.64 at the start of its inner loop, then writes it back. Total unique read footprint = 57,657,600 × 8 = 461,260,800 bytes ≈ 440 MB. The L2 cache is 40 MB, so the read footprint far exceeds L2. Nearly all reads will go to DRAM. Total DRAM bytes read ≈ 461,260,800 bytes. Note: result_wo was allocated with map(alloc:) and memset was done on host before the target data region, but the data was not mapped to device (map alloc doesn't transfer). However, the first kernel invoked on result_wo is this kernel (woAtomicOnGlobalMem), and the memory was zero-initialized on host but map(alloc) means no transfer. The device memory is uninitialized. The kernel still reads it via LDG. So 461,260,800 bytes read from DRAM.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each thread writes one double (8 bytes) back to result[] via STG.E.64. Total unique write footprint = 57,657,600 × 8 = 461,260,800 bytes ≈ 440 MB. This far exceeds the 40 MB L2 cache, so most writes will be evicted to DRAM during kernel execution. DRAM bytes written ≈ 461,260,800 bytes.
